headings: ### When to Change the Strategy (not in yet)

rows.label: P1 · draft (alone 100% AI, medium)
rows.text: If you've been at something for weeks and not much is changing, I think part of you might be hoping someone will just tell you to quit, and part of you might be scared to. Before either, I'd check whether you actually did the part you meant to practice, or mostly read about it and got ready to (reading this counts as getting ready). And if it was comforting your little one, was the loving grown-up really there? Your little one would notice if it wasn't, the way you notice a hug from someone who's checking their phone. I'd borrow that grown-up first. Then try again, and see if your little one can tell the difference.

source.quote: If you keep trying something and not much seems to change, don’t immediately decide the whole method has failed—and don’t protect it by repeating the same thing forever either. First find out what actually happened.
source.from: the updated guide, When to Change the Strategy

source.quote: Did you really get to the step you meant to practice, or did you mostly think, read, talk, or prepare for it? Was the adult function you needed actually available? Did fear, distrust, confusion, exhaustion, lack of skill, a practical barrier, or a protective part get in the way? If one concrete blockage shows up, work on that blockage and keep the larger goal.
source.from: the updated guide, When to Change the Strategy

source.quote: For example, if you are trying to comfort the child but the loving adult position is not really there yet, the next move may be to borrow that adult function first—not to force more loving sentences at the child and not to declare reparenting useless. Then try the adjusted version and decide beforehand what small change would tell you it helped.
source.from: the updated guide, When to Change the Strategy

rows.note: Six versions. With a joke, 😅 and the hug picture it was AI, high, and so were both halves. Rewritten around what you and your little one are thinking it dropped to medium and stayed there through a new opener and a new last line.

rows.label: P2 · draft (alone 100% Human, high)
rows.text: How many tries is enough? I really don't know, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who gives you a number, since some things shift in a day and some take about as long as learning guitar. If it's making things worse, or you just can't do it right now, I'd change course sooner. Not wanting to do it anymore can count too, but I'd hear that no out first, sudden or not, since it might be a part of you that's trying to protect you. And if what it said would happen keeps not happening when you're doing it right, I think you've learned something real about it. A clearly better-supported way is worth switching for too.

source.quote: Some effects should be visible quickly; others are skills that develop through repetition. Don’t invent a magic number of attempts. Change or stop the approach sooner when it is making things worse, you genuinely don’t want to do it, it is not feasible, the target turns out to be wrong, or something the method specifically predicted should happen keeps failing under the conditions where it was supposed to happen. A clearly better-supported route is also a reason to switch.
source.from: the updated guide, When to Change the Strategy

rows.label: P3 · draft (alone 100% Human, high)
rows.text: The trap I'd watch for is explaining away every miss. It didn't work, so you must have done it wrong, so maybe you needed the right candle first. Next time it's something else, and none of it is anything you actually noticed while you were doing it. At some point nothing could prove the method wrong.

source.quote: One more trap: don’t define “I did it correctly” as “it worked.” And don’t add a new invisible prerequisite every time it disappoints you. The point of reviewing the strategy is to learn what is actually helping, what is blocked, and what should change next—not to make the method impossible to disprove.
source.from: the updated guide, When to Change the Strategy
